title: COP31 hosts table final climate deal that still does not name fossil fuels
dek: The Antalya text keeps a 35% electrification goal and calls for faster carbon capture, but drops a dollar target for adaptation finance. A session to approve it was due at 11.30 am IST on Sunday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The hosts of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, put forward what they called a final text early on Sunday, two days after the talks were due to end, and asked nearly 200 countries to approve it. The draft makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels, the central dispute of the two-week meeting, and instead alludes to the 2023 agreement at COP28 in Dubai to shift away from them, according to reports.

"We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon," Murat Kurum, the COP31 president and Türkiye's environment minister, told a late-night plenary on Saturday. Delegations had until 3 am GMT (8.30 am IST) to lodge objections, and a session to begin approving the deal was scheduled for 6 am GMT (11.30 am IST), according to reports. At the closing plenary later on Sunday the text was not adopted, after the European Union and Panama formally objected; Mr Kurum said there was "no consensus on this document" (see our later report). UN climate decisions need consensus, so a single formal objection can block or delay adoption.

## What the text says

According to reports on the drafts, the package:

- keeps a proposal to raise electricity's share of the world's final energy use from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035, now framed as one of several options for "global cooperation" rather than a call on each country
- calls for "accelerating" carbon capture and storage, which Mr Kurum has called an "important priority" and which many countries and scientists say is expensive and unproven at scale
- calls on countries to "at least triple adaptation finance by 2035", having dropped a $120 billion target from an earlier version, and acknowledges adaptation needs of about $305 billion a year
- sets up an "Antalya-to-Addis Ababa Roadmap" that leaves the detail to COP32 in Ethiopia next year

An earlier version of the same text described an "irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions" in place of the COP28 wording on "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems", and removed a call to phase out inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies. If approved, the deal would also be the first COP decision to acknowledge that warming is on course to pass the 1.5°C limit set in Paris in 2015, according to reports.

## Who objects

A group led by France and Panama, including Belgium, Côte d'Ivoire, Finland, Greece, Guatemala, Spain, Sweden and Vanuatu, said on Friday that the agreement then on the table was not good enough, the UN reported. Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said: "It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels." Panama has threatened to formally object unless its demands, including a cap on oil production, are met. Ireland's climate minister said around 130 countries wanted at least a reference to fossil fuels, according to reports.

Saudi Arabia and other oil producers objected to fossil-fuel language in the first draft, which was then removed. The EU's climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, said on Saturday that "it's better to have no deal than to have a bad deal", according to reports. Mohamed Adow of the Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa said the summit risked being a "ghost COP".

The UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, told leaders in Antalya earlier that "polluters must pay" and called for adaptation funding to be tripled by 2035.

## Why it matters for India

India has said it will not accept new obligations, has opposed an electrification pledge and a fossil-fuel phase-out roadmap, and has pressed rich countries to deliver finance. A text without fossil-fuel language and without a dollar figure for adaptation meets India's first concern but not its second. Finance is the practical question for low-lying coasts such as the Sundarbans in Bengal, where cyclones and saline flooding have damaged embankments and farmland. India had not commented publicly on the final text by Sunday afternoon.

## What happens next

If no country formally objects, Mr Kurum can declare the package adopted. Only one COP, in The Hague in 2000, has ended without a decision. This report will be updated with the outcome of the closing session.
